bc_mount_lapworth.blurb: Mount Lapworth is a mountain-top crag in the Sea to Sky corridor near Squamish, set high on a peak away from the main Squamish walls. It has five trad routes of about three pitches each, running from 5.7 up to 5.10, with two at 5.9 and two at 5.10. The wall faces north, which keeps it cool and makes it a candidate for hot summer days. Several routes mix bolted slab pitches with crack and corner climbing, so bring a single to double rack along with quickdraws, and a 70 m rope. Anchors sit at the top of the climbs. Expect a full mountain day rather than a quick crag visit.

bc_chipmunk_creek_wall.blurb: Chipmunk Creek Wall is a small sport crag in the Fraser Valley near Chilliwack, on the Chilliwack Lake side of the valley. It has five bolted single-pitch routes, all in the hard range: three around 5.11 and two at 5.12. Some lines are short, while the longest run roughly 45 to 50 m and need around 18 to 20 quickdraws and a 60 m rope. The wall faces southwest and rises above a shaded valley, so the top-outs catch the late sun on summer evenings. This is a destination for stronger sport climbers rather than beginners; a helmet is worth wearing on the trail below the wall.

bc_prison_crag.blurb: Prison Crag is a compact sport crag in the Fraser Valley, up the Chilliwack Lake road from Chilliwack. Five bolted single-pitch routes climb a south-facing wall that dries quickly after rain. Grades step upward one climb at a time from 5.7 to 5.11, which makes it handy for a mixed group: a couple of easier warm-ups, a mid-grade line, and one hard route. A 60 m rope reaches the ground from every line, and the bolts are glue-ins, so carry a bail biner just in case.

bc_khartoum.blurb: Khartoum is a big multipitch wall in the upper Lois Valley, beyond Khartoum Lake and south of Powell River, with Mt. Diadem at the head of the valley. There are five trad routes, from a three-pitch 5.7 to climbs of 8 and 9 pitches around 5.9 and 5.10. The wall faces east, so it loses the sun in the afternoon during summer. Its crack systems are broken up by technical face climbing, and the rock is clean by coastal standards, with knobby chickenheads. Plan on a long day, since most of the lines are well over a few pitches, and expect to stay at the camp in the valley.

bc_mt_habrich.blurb: Mt. Habrich is a granite horn east of Squamish, a committing alpine objective rather than a roadside crag. Five trad routes are known here, from a 5.8 up to a 5.13 on the north face, with most of the rest around 5.10. The longest is a 27-pitch link-up that finishes on the summit; the others run from about five to ten pitches. The rock is well featured and generally good, and the views from the route and the top are big. Most parties start from the Sea to Sky gondola and walk in for about two hours. Several parties on the same route is not unusual on summer weekends.

bc_tower_of_tails.blurb: Tower of Tails is a small tower of roughly 40 m with walls around it, up in the Okanagan hills at about 1,100 m elevation. It has five trad routes, from 5.7 to 5.10, with the two hardest at 5.10. The climbing is cracks and faces; the rock is excellent on the steep and overhanging sections but mossy and loose on the lower-angle ground, so test holds and wear a helmet. It is a remote spot reached by a long forest road, so you will likely have it to yourself. Bring a standard trad rack, since the routes are short and protected by gear.

bc_rampage_rock.blurb: Rampage Rock is a small south-facing crag above the Valleycliffe neighbourhood of Squamish, about 15 m tall and shaped like a half-dome. Five trad routes follow its cracks, with grades from 5.6 up to 5.10, one in each step, so it suits a newer leader as well as someone after a short session. The two central hand cracks are the obvious lines. The placements are on the technical side, so bring plenty of small nuts. Moss covers much of the face. Each line ends at a single staple, so carry a cordalette to equalize and expect to clean a route before you climb it.
